stem: A research lab's compliance policy states that Amazon S3 must never receive or store the plaintext encryption key for a dataset, and the lab's own key-management system, not AWS, must supply a unique key on every upload and download request. Which encryption option meets this requirement?

choices.text: SSE-KMS using a customer managed key
SSE-C, with the key supplied by the caller on every request
SSE-S3 with the default Amazon S3 managed key
DSSE-KMS with an S3 Bucket Key enabled

rationale: SSE-C has S3 perform the encryption but requires the caller to supply the raw key on every request, and S3 never stores that key, which matches a policy that keeps the key entirely under the lab's own key-management system. SSE-KMS still relies on AWS KMS to hold and use the key material on the lab's behalf, even with a customer managed key, so the key material is still inside an AWS-operated service. SSE-S3 uses a key that Amazon S3 manages entirely, which is the opposite of the lab supplying its own key. DSSE-KMS also depends on AWS KMS-generated key material for one of its two encryption layers, and S3 Bucket Keys are not even supported for DSSE-KMS, so neither detail satisfies a policy demanding a caller-supplied key.
